extracted.intended_audience: American statesmen / educated American public (readers considering constitutional design)
extracted.subtask_description: Historical-political guidance for evaluating and designing republican constitutions, drawn from ancient Greek examples; emphasizes mixed government, checks and balances, confederation design, and the dangers of faction, fragmentation, and reliance on slavery or foreign allies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective balance of three powers (king, senate, assembly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Would Mr. Turgot have said, that if Thebes, Athens, Argos, and the Achaian, Arcadian, and Olynthian leagues, had been each of them governed by a legislature composed of a king, senate, and assembly, with equal authority, and each a decisive negative...?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues for a government composed of three independent orders (monarchy, aristocracy, democracy) with equal authority and each possessing a decisive negative (veto) over the others. This balance is presented as the remedy to perpetual factional revolutions evident in Greek cities; Romans and England are cited as examples of attempts to realize such a balance. Anti-pattern: single-order systems (pure democracy, oligarchy, monarchy) that lack this mutual negative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of mixture and decisive balances to prevent cyclical revolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle...shows the greater necessity of mixtures of different orders, and decisive balances, to preserve mankind from those horrible calamities which revolutions always bring with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawing on Aristotle and Plato, the page asserts that simple governments tend to change into their opposites (monarchy→oligarchy→democracy→tyranny, etc.). Therefore constitutions should mix orders and embed clear checks so that no single faction can completely overturn the system. Example: recommending mixture to avoid the 'circle' of revolutions seen across Greek polities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fragmentation into many tiny sovereign states
rubrics_metrics.description: Would the childlish humour of separating into as many States as towns have ever been indulged or permitted? Most certainly they would not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns that making every town a sovereign independent democracy leads to persistent wars, alliances, and intrigues among them. Small, numerous sovereign units lack the leisure and resources to sustain stable politics and will devolve into factional conflicts and external entanglements. Anti-pattern: proposing extreme local sovereignty without unifying mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small cities require continual combined force and common interest to survive
rubrics_metrics.description: That small cities could be preserved by nothing else but a continual and combined force, united by the bond of common interest; and, as the members of the body live and breathe by their mutual communication and connection... they enjoy the benefit of that providence and council that governs the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Achaian confederacy is cited as an example: small towns preserved their independence and checked ambition by uniting under common assemblies and shared interests. Recommendation: confederation or union with shared institutions and mutual interests to keep small polities viable. Anti-pattern: isolated small states 'putrify' once separated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusive citizenship and common institutions (laws, weights, measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: They admitted strangers into their community on equal terms with the ancient citizens... having common laws and institutions, and common weights and measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achaia is praised for admitting 'strangers' on equal terms and having uniform laws and measures; such inclusivity and standardization are presented as strengths for confederated republics. Guidance: promote equal admission, uniform legal/economic standards across member units to reduce internal domination by a single capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotation of magistracies and accountability of generals
rubrics_metrics.description: Their congresses annually appointed presidents in rotation, and generals, who were responsible to the congress, as the members of congress were to the cities they represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional mechanisms like short terms and rotation of executives, plus military commanders made responsible to representative bodies, help check ambition and prevent accumulation of personal power. Example: Achaia's rotating 'praetors' and accountable generals. Anti-pattern: long-lived tyrannies or unchecked military leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constituent units must have mixed internal constitutions for confederation to work
rubrics_metrics.description: If the cities represented in it had been well constituted of a mixture of three independent powers: — But it is plain they were not; but were in a continual struggle between their first magistrates, nobles, and people, for superiority, which occasioned their short duration, and final ruin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A confederal congress will perform well only if the cities that compose it have internal balances (mixed constitutions). Without internal checks, local factionalism undermines the larger union. Example: Achaia's congress could have governed foreign affairs well 'if the cities represented had been well constituted'—they were not, leading to instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not allow internal factions to invite foreign intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: Each faction... applied to foreign powers; the regal party applied to Macedonian kings, the aristocratical citizens applied to Sparta, and the democratical factions applied to Aratus and the Achaian league.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When domestic parties seek external patrons, the result is foreign garrisons, occupations, and massacres. Constitutional design should reduce incentives for factions to appeal to outside powers (e.g., by providing fair channels for competition and redress). Anti-pattern: factions dependent on foreign military support.

rubrics_metrics.name: General assembly must be active and authoritative
rubrics_metrics.description: The general assembly was neglected; the cities became independent: some were conquered by foreigners, and some lost their liberties by domestic tyrants...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a confederation, the central assembly must be respected and active; its neglect permits member units to drift, invite tyrants, or fall to outside powers. Example: the Achaian general assembly's neglect led to fragmentation. Recommendation: ensure participation and enforcement mechanisms for central bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid systems dependent on mass slavery or exclusionary freemen determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Let every town in the Thirteen States be a Uqq sovereign and independent democracy; here you may nearly collect all authority into one center, and that center the nation. The first step to be taken then, is to determine who shall be freemen, and who slaves. Let this be determined by lot. In every fifty men, forty are to be slaves... The other ten are to be free citizens...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage uses a hypothetical/satirical model to show how certain republican arrangements presuppose a large enslaved class and extreme inequalities. It warns against constitutional designs that rely on unfree labor or arbitrary exclusion to sustain civic leisure and military capacity. Anti-pattern: building political liberty on mass unfreedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic capacity to support defense and public service matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Wars did not cost money in Greece... An American soldier will not serve one year, without more money for pay than many of these Greek cities had for their whole circulating medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern republican design must account for the fiscal capacity necessary to maintain armies, public service, and institutions. Systems that rely on unpaid militia or slave labor are unsuited to contemporary requirements. Recommendation: ensure sustainable public finance and compensation for service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public education, austerity, and military training as instruments of order (with trade-offs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Their education, which was public, was directed to make them soldiers. The youth were restrained to a rigid temperance, modesty, and morality, enforced by law... Such regulations could not fail to secure order, and what they called freedom to the citizens; but nine-tenths of mankind were doomed to slavery to support them in total idleness...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civic education and social discipline can promote order and military effectiveness (example: Cretan/Minos system). However, the text warns of severe moral and human costs and instability resulting from systems that secure citizens' leisure via mass servitude. Trade-off: order vs. equality and liberty for all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent domination by a single powerful capital within a confederation
rubrics_metrics.description: In all other states of Greece, in which the people had any share in government, there were constant complaints, that one powerful capital domineered over the inferior towns and villages, like Thebes in Boeotia, Athens in Attica.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unequal economic or political centralization permits a capital to dominate and undercut the federation. Good confederation design should check the ambition of dominant cities (through balanced representation, shared institutions, or structural equality among members). Example: Achaia's lack of a commercial capital helped equality among member towns.
